title: Metrology and quality control: measuring parts and control charts
examples: How do I calculate Cp and Cpk?
What is the difference between a vernier caliper and a micrometer?

explain.say: A car engine has thousands of parts that must fit, made in different factories in different countries. That only works because everyone measures the same way. Metrology is the science of measurement. Look at the board: how finely common tools can read, from a steel rule down to a coordinate measuring machine.

draw.text: Metrology and quality control: measuring parts and control charts
Resolution: the smallest step an instrument can show

explain.say: A vernier caliper reads to 0.02 millimetres, a micrometer to 0.01, and a CMM to about a micrometre. A good rule of thumb is the rule of ten: the instrument should resolve a tenth of the tolerance. For a shaft of 25 plus or minus 0.03 millimetres, the tolerance band is 0.06, so which tool would you pick?

A micrometer, since 0.06 over 10 is 0.006, and a caliper is too coarse. Now quality control. Measuring every part tells you about the past; a control chart warns you about the future. See the graph: shaft diameters in order, with control limits three standard deviations either side of the mean.

Points wander randomly inside the limits: that is normal variation. Sample 11, at 25.02 millimetres, jumps above the upper limit. It is still inside the 25.03 tolerance, but the process has changed. Maybe the tool is wearing. See it? What should the operator do?

draw.text: A point outside the limits signals a special cause

explain.say: Stop, find the cause and fix it, then keep watching: the cycle on the board. Superb. Capability measures how well the process fits the tolerance: Cp is tolerance over 6 sigma, 0.06 over 0.03, which is 2. If the mean drifts to 25.01, Cpk drops to 1.33. Exam tip: Cpk of at least 1.33 is a common target.

faq.q: What is the difference between a vernier caliper and a micrometer?
faq.a: A vernier caliper reads to about 0.02 millimetres and measures inside, outside and depth. A micrometer uses a fine screw to read to 0.01 millimetres or better, but over a short range.

A graph of a measured feature over time with a centre line and control limits, usually three standard deviations either side. Points outside the limits or odd patterns signal that the process has changed.
asks: what does a control chart show

faq.a: Lines set at the process mean plus and minus three standard deviations. They describe what the process normally does, which is not the same as the tolerance limits on the drawing.

faq.q: What should I do when a point goes out of control?
faq.a: Stop and look for a special cause, such as tool wear, a temperature change or a new material batch, fix it, record it, and carry on charting.

faq.q: How do I calculate Cp and Cpk?
faq.a: Cp equals the tolerance width divided by 6 sigma. Cpk equals the distance from the mean to the nearer limit divided by 3 sigma, so it also penalises an off-centre process.

facts: Control limits are usually set at the mean ± 3 standard deviations.
A Cpk of 1.33 or more is a common capability target in manufacturing.

quiz.say: A part has limits 10.00 plus or minus 0.05 millimetres. The process has sigma 0.01 and a centred mean. What is Cp?
quiz.show: Tolerance 10.00 ± 0.05 mm, σ = 0.01 mm, centred. Cp?

wrong.1: That divides 6σ by the tolerance, upside down.
wrong.2: That uses only σ instead of 6σ.

quiz.why: Control limits describe normal variation; a point beyond them signals a special cause even if the part still passes.

wrong.1: The part passes today, but the process is drifting and may soon make scrap.
wrong.2: The limits come from the process data; the point is the warning.
